title: Quantitative Trait Loci and Heritability
markdown: ## What this covers This chapter is built from the lecture 19 slide deck of MIT's 7.091J (*Foundations of Computational and Systems Biology*), given by David Gifford; no transcript, written notes or problem set were supplied for this session, so the exposition follows the deck's own ordering and spells out the reasoning the slides only sketch. It answers: given that relatives resemble each other more than random members of a population do, how much of that resemblance can be attributed to shared genotype (heritability), and can a quantitative trait be predicted directly from genetic markers (QTL mapping)? It assumes basic probability — mean, variance, the binomial distribution — and the idea of a genetic cross between two parental strains. ## Where the lecture picked up The deck opens with two slides finishing material from the previous session, before a "Today's Narrative Arc" slide marks the actual start of this lecture. They are recorded here for completeness, but nothing connects them to the QTL material that follows. **5C** (Chromosome Conformation Capture Carbon Copy) extends 3C to map physical contacts between many pairs of genomic loci at once. The workflow: cross-link interacting loci inside the nucleus, digest with a restriction enzyme, ligate the cross-linked fragments, and reverse the cross-links to recover a "3C library" of ligated fragment pairs. That library is then annealed to a multiplexed panel of alternating forward (T7) and reverse (T3) primers tiled across a genomic region of interest; the annealed primers are themselves ligated wherever their target fragments were adjacent in the 3C library, the products are amplified by PCR with universal T7/T3 primers, and the amplicons are read out by sequencing or microarray. The detectable pairwise ligation products between primer pairs are drawn as arcs above and below the tiled region (Dostie & Dekker, 2007). **DNA methylation** is the addition of a methyl group to a cytosine within a CpG dinucleotide, concentrated in gene regulatory regions. It silences genes by blocking the binding of regulatory factors and by affecting chromatin state. It is also copied across cell division: an unmethylated CpG cluster can be methylated de novo by a DNA methyltransferase (DNMT), and after DNA replication produces a hemimethylated cluster (methylated on only one strand) that DNMT restores to full methylation — a maintenance step that makes the mark a heritable, lasting form of epigenetic information. ## From genotype to phenotype - **Genotype**: an individual's complete genome sequence, or — in practice — an approximation given by markers at specific genomic sites recording differences from a reference genome. - **Phenotype**: one or more measured traits. A trait can be non-quantitative (dead/alive) or quantitative — fitness (growth rate, lifespan), morphology (height), or gene expression level. - A **quantitative trait locus (QTL)** is a marker statistically associated with a quantitative trait. When the trait is a gene's expression level, the marker is called an **eQTL**. Why this matters practically: computational models that predict phenotype from genotype are the basis for understanding disease-associated genomic variants and for choosing the most effective therapy for a given patient (pharmacogenomics). The rest of the lecture builds one such model — predicting a quantitative phenotype by summing the contributions of individual QTLs — and then asks how well it actually works. ## A statistics refresher Two quantities do all the work in what follows: the variance of a single variable and the covariance between two. $$\mu_x = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N} x_i \qquad \sigma_x^2 = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\left(x_i-\mu_x\right)^2 = E\left[(X-\mu_x)^2\right]$$ $$\sigma_{xy}^2 = E\left[(X-\mu_x)(Y-\mu_y)\right]$$ with $\sigma_{xy}^2 = 0$ when $X$ and $Y$ are independent. ## Two toy genetic models ### Binary haploid model: all-or-nothing Cross two haploid parents at $N$ marker loci. Every marker on one parent's genome is "empty" (not needed for the phenotype); every marker on the other's is "filled" (needed for the phenotype). An F1 offspring inherits, independently at each locus, one parent's allele or the other's with probability $1/2$ each. If the phenotype (say, survival in a given environment) requires the filled allele at every one of the $N$ loci at once, an F1 shows it only when all $N$ independent coin flips land on "filled" — probability $(1/2)^N$. The observed fraction of F1s with the phenotype therefore estimates $(1/2)^N$, and inverting gives an estimate of how many loci are involved: $$N \approx \log_2\!\left(\frac{\#\ \text{F1s tested}}{\#\ \text{F1s with phenotype}}\right).$$ ### Quantitative haploid model: additive, small effects Replace the all-or-nothing requirement with a small additive contribution: each locus contributes effect size $0$ if inherited from one parent and $1/N$ if inherited from the other (phenotype example: growth rate). The phenotype score is then the fraction of loci inherited from the "effect" parent, i.e. $k/N$ for $k \sim \text{Binomial}(N, 0.5)$: $$p(x,N) = \binom{N}{x}(0.5)^{N-x}(0.5)^{x}, \qquad E[x] = 0.5, \qquad \sigma_x^2 = \frac{0.25}{N}.$$ Overlaying this binomial mass function on a normal density with the same mean and variance shows the two converging as $N$ grows — the central limit theorem: a phenotype built from many independent loci of small additive effect looks approximately normal even though any single locus is a discrete coin flip. This is the picture underneath the additive model used for the rest of the lecture: real quantitative traits are typically modeled as roughly normal precisely because they are built from many small-effect loci, not because there is anything intrinsically continuous about a genotype. ## Linkage makes nearby markers correlated Two markers sitting close together on the same chromosome are unlikely to be separated by a crossover during meiosis, so an F1 tends to inherit them together rather than independently. In practice, this means a genome scan for QTLs will often show several significant, tightly clustered markers flanking one true causal locus, rather than several independent causal loci — the correlation is a mapping-resolution effect of physical proximity, not necessarily evidence of several distinct QTLs. ## Phenotype as genotype plus environment For an individual $i$ with genotype $g_i$ and quantitative phenotype $p_i$, write the phenotype as a function of genotype plus an environmental term $e_i$: $$p_i = f(g_i) + e_i, \qquad \sigma_p^2 = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\left(p_i-\mu_p\right)^2.$$ Variance decomposes as $$\sigma_p^2 = \sigma_g^2 + \sigma_e^2 + 2\sigma_{ge}^2, \qquad E[e_i]=0,\quad E[e_i^2]=\sigma_e^2,$$ and if genotype and environment are independent (or made so by the experimental design), the cross term vanishes: $$\sigma_p^2 = \sigma_g^2 + \sigma_e^2.$$ ## Two heritabilities, and why both exist - **Broad-sense** heritability describes the upper bound on phenotype prediction by an *optimal, arbitrary* model of genotype, so it reflects the full complexity of the underlying molecular mechanism. - **Narrow-sense** heritability describes the upper bound on phenotype prediction by a *linear (additive)* model of genotype. It is what governs family resemblance — additive effects are what is transmitted predictably from parent to offspring — and what makes genetic mapping studies tractable. A few caveats worth keeping attached to both numbers: heritability is a property of a specific population (its segregating allele frequencies) and a specific environment (its noise level), not a fixed property of a trait in the abstract; the bare word "heritability" in the literature can mean either the broad- or narrow-sense version, or silently assume the two are equal; and both are hard to estimate cleanly, since doing so requires matching environments and avoiding confounding. ## Broad-sense heritability, $H^2$ $$H^2 = \frac{\sigma_g^2}{\sigma_p^2} = \frac{\sigma_p^2 - \sigma_e^2}{\sigma_p^2}.$$ $\sigma_e^2$ can be estimated directly from genetically identical individuals — clones, or identical twins — since any phenotypic variance observed among them must be purely environmental. Worked example (reproduced on the slide from Hartl's *Essential Genetics*): three genotype classes ($aa$, $Aa$, $AA$) each have their own phenotype distribution. With no environmental variation at all, those three distributions are narrow and well separated, giving $\sigma_g^2 = 2.0$. Adding environmental noise on top of a single genotype gives a distribution with $\sigma_e^2 = 1.0$. Combining both — real genotypes plus real environmental noise — gives the observed phenotype distribution, with $\sigma_p^2 = \sigma_g^2+\sigma_e^2 = 3.0$, hence $$H^2 = \frac{2.0}{3.0} = \frac{2}{3}.$$ ## The additive model and Galton's regression to the mean Restrict attention to markers identified as QTLs and model phenotype as linear in the (0/1-coded) genotype at each: $$f_a(g_i) = \sum_{j\in\text{QTL}} \beta_j g_{ij} + \beta_0.$$ Because $f_a$ is linear, and each locus in a haploid offspring is inherited from one parent or the other with probability $1/2$ independently, its expectation is exactly the midpoint of what the two parents would score: $$E[f_a(g_i)] = \frac{f_a(p_1)}{2} + \frac{f_a(p_2)}{2}.$$ Children are therefore expected to sit near the midpoint of their parents under a purely additive model — the same phenomenon Galton described from mid-parent versus offspring height in 1886: the deviation of children from the population mean is, on average, only about $2/3$ of the mid-parent's deviation ("regression toward mediocrity" — mid-parents taller than average have children who tend to be shorter than they are, and vice versa). The slope of offspring phenotype regressed on mid-parent phenotype in a plot like Galton's is the historical, pre-formal ancestor of the narrow-sense heritability defined next. ## Narrow-sense heritability, $h^2$ Fit the additive model $f_a$ to the data and measure the fraction of phenotypic variance it captures: $$p_i = f_a(g_i) + e_i, \qquad \sigma_a^2 = \sigma_p^2 - \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\left(p_i - f_a(g_i)\right)^2, \qquad h^2 = \frac{\sigma_a^2}{\sigma_p^2}.$$ The additive model is a restricted special case of the fully general model that defines $H^2$, so it can never explain more variance than the general model does: $\sigma_a^2 \le \sigma_g^2$, hence $h^2 \le H^2$ always. The gap between the two is variance that is genetic — it shows up in $H^2$ — but not additive, so a linear QTL model cannot find it. That gap is exactly what the rest of this chapter calls "missing heritability." Reported narrow-sense heritabilities vary widely by trait: human height $\approx 0.8$, cattle yearling weight $\approx 0.35$, *Drosophila* life history $\approx 0.2$, wild-animal life history $\approx 0.3$ (Visscher et al., 2008), with wider surveys across morphological and fitness traits in several species showing the same trait-to-trait spread. ## Finding QTLs: the LOD score test To decide whether a marker $j$ is a QTL for a trait, compare two models of the trait's distribution across individuals: one where the mean depends on which allele the individual carries at marker $j$ ($\mu_0$ for one allele, $\mu_1$ for the other, shared variance $\sigma$), against a null model with a single population mean $\mu$ regardless of genotype. The LOD score is the log-likelihood ratio between them, accumulated over all $N$ individuals: $$LOD = \log_{10}\prod_{i=1}^{N} \frac{P\left(p_i \mid g_{ij},\mu_0,\mu_1,\sigma\right)}{P\left(p_i \mid \mu,\sigma\right)}.$$ A large LOD score means the marker-conditioned model fits much better than the unconditioned one. To calibrate what counts as "large," permute the genotype-to-phenotype assignment 1000 times — breaking any real association — and recompute the LOD score each time to build an empirical null distribution; pick the threshold on that null distribution corresponding to a false discovery rate of $0.05$, and apply it to the real, unpermuted genome scan to call significant QTLs. Having found a set of QTLs, fit a linear (additive) model using them, subtract its prediction from the phenotype, and repeat the whole search on the residuals — iterated up to three times — to pick up additional QTLs whose signal was masked by the ones already found. ## Case study: a yeast cross with about 1000 segregants Bloom, Ehrenreich, Loo, Võ Lite & Kruglyak, "Finding the sources of missing heritability in a yeast cross" (*Nature*, 2013), ran this machinery at a scale that let them ask directly where missing heritability lives. Two haploid yeast strains, BY and RM, were mated, the resulting diploid was taken through meiosis, and dissecting the resulting tetrads gave a panel of about 1,000 haploid segregants, each an independent reshuffling of the two parental genomes. Growth of every segregant was measured under 46 different conditions (sugars; drugs such as Congo Red, Zeocin, Neomycin, Cisplatin, Caffeine, Menadione; ethanol; and others), and every segregant was sequenced to call, at each SNP, which parent's haplotype it carried. Some of the 46 traits correlate with each other — a cluster of sugar-growth traits together with growth on 2% ethanol stood out as an example — itself evidence that they share some underlying genetic architecture. Scaling the panel up mattered enormously for detection power. For growth in the drug E6 berbamine, the full panel of 1,005 segregants found 15 significant QTLs, jointly explaining 78% of that trait's narrow-sense heritability; a subsample of only 100 segregants found just 2 significant QTLs, explaining 21%. Sample size, not biology, was the binding constraint on how much of $h^2$ could actually be found. With QTLs in hand, a cross-validated additive model built from them predicted phenotype well out of sample — 22 QTLs for growth in lithium chloride explained 88% of that trait's narrow-sense heritability, with predicted values landing close to observed values across segregants. Across all 46 traits, the number of detected QTLs ranged from 5 to 29 (median 12), most of them individually small in effect — a histogram of effect sizes pooled across traits looks like a truncated exponential, matching the "many loci, small additive effects" picture from the toy model above. Two results together set up the rest of the lecture. First, plotting the phenotypic variance explained by the detected QTLs against each trait's estimated $h^2$, the points fall close to the diagonal — for most traits the additive QTL model captures essentially all of the narrow-sense heritability (72–100% across traits). Second, plotting each trait's $h^2$ against its $H^2$, every point falls **below** the $h^2 = H^2$ diagonal, consistently, across all 46 traits. So the additive model is doing about as well as an additive model possibly can here — the shortfall is not a mapping power problem, since more segregants closed that kind of gap in the berbamine example above. It is that $h^2$ itself sits well below $H^2$: the vertical gap between them is non-additive genetic variance the linear model was never going to catch, no matter how many segregants were added. ## What causes missing heritability? The lecture lists several, non-exclusive candidates: incorrect heritability estimates, non-chromosomal inheritance, rare variants, structural variants, many common variants each of small effect (a detection-power problem, as the berbamine comparison shows), and epistasis (gene–gene interaction). Epistasis is worth working through, because it produces a case where the entire trait is genetically determined and yet an additive, single-marker search finds nothing. Consider two loci $A$ and $B$, each with two alleles, and a phenotype function: | | $b$ | $B$ | | --- | --- | --- | | $a$ | $f(ab)=0$ | $f(aB)=1$ | | $A$ | $f(Ab)=1$ | $f(AB)=0$ | The phenotype is $1$ exactly when the two loci disagree, $0$ when they agree. Averaging over the other locus, switching $a\to A$ changes the phenotype by $+1$ when paired with $b$ and by $-1$ when paired with $B$; if the cross makes $b$ and $B$ equally likely, the average effect of substituting the allele at $A$ is exactly zero — and symmetrically for $B$. Neither locus shows any effect on its own, so neither is detected as a QTL, and an additive model built from the two explains none of the variance: with no environmental noise, $H^2=1$ (phenotype is fully determined by genotype) but $h^2=0$ (the additive model captures none of it). Broad-sense heritability, recall, folds in additive effects, dominance, gene–gene interactions, gene–environment interactions and non-genomic inheritance; narrow-sense heritability only ever sees the first of these. Testing for interactions directly is possible in principle, but considering all combinations of markers — all pairs, let alone higher-order combinations — is in general intractable once the multiple-hypothesis correction that many tests demands is accounted for. In the yeast panel, a genome-wide search for pairwise QTL–QTL interactions did find real ones, but they closed the $h^2$–$H^2$ gap for only a few traits: growth in maltose stood out, where a single interaction between QTLs on chromosomes 7 and 11 explained 71% of that trait's gap. For most of the 46 traits, the detected pairwise interactions left most of the non-additive variance unaccounted for — consistent with the combinatorial search problem just described. A second, distinct source of missing heritability comes from Edwards, Symbor-Nagrabska et al., "Interactions between chromosomal and nonchromosomal elements reveal missing heritability" (*PNAS*, 2014): some yeast phenotypes depend on a cytoplasmic, non-chromosomal element — the [KIL-k] versus [KIL-0] killer state — that is not part of the genome sequence at all, and so is invisible to any QTL scan built on SNP genotypes. For the gene PEP7, a model built only from the chromosomal deletion explains little of the phenotype; adding the non-chromosomal element as a second, additive predictor explains more; but only a model that adds an explicit interaction term between the deletion and the non-chromosomal element removes the remaining gap between the mutant and wild-type phenotype distributions. Missing heritability, here, was hiding in an interaction with something outside the genome being sequenced at all. ## The human motivation The same shortfall shows up, at much larger scale, in human disease genetics. After hundreds of genome-wide association studies, the loci found for a given complex disease or trait typically explain only a small fraction of its estimated heritability (Manolio, Collins et al., "Finding the missing heritability of complex diseases," *Nature*, 2009): | Disease / trait | Loci found | Heritability explained | | --- | --- | --- | | Age-related macular degeneration | 5 | 50% | | Crohn's disease | 32 | 20% | | Systemic lupus erythematosus | 6 | 15% | | Type 2 diabetes | 18 | 6% | | HDL cholesterol | 7 | 5.2% | | Height | 40 | 5% | | Early-onset myocardial infarction | 9 | 2.8% | | Fasting glucose | 4 | 1.5% | This table is the practical stakes behind the lecture's opening claim: predicting phenotype from genotype matters for disease-associated variants and pharmacogenomics, and missing heritability is the main obstacle currently standing in the way. ## Where to look next The lecture closes this as an open problem rather than a solved one: use external annotation of markers (SNPs known to sit in enhancers, nonsense mutations, and similar functional evidence) to shrink the search space before testing for non-linear interactions, since testing all combinations of markers is otherwise intractable; explicitly consider non-chromosomal genetic elements, which a sequence-only genotype scan will never see; and use complementary data — protein–protein interaction networks, for instance — to decide which interactions are worth testing rather than testing all of them combinatorially. ## Sources Everything above is drawn from the single supplied source: the slide deck `docs/computational-biology/mit-ocw/7091j/lectures/19-slides.md` (MIT OCW 7.091J / 20.490J / 20.390J / 7.36J / 6.802J / 6.874J / HST.506J, *Foundations of Computational and Systems Biology*, Spring 2014, lecture 19, David Gifford). No transcript, written notes or problem set were supplied for this lecture, so no exercises section could be added, and no spoken commentary supplements the slide text; the reasoning above (the log2 and midpoint derivations, the CLT reading of the binomial plot, the $h^2 \le H^2$ argument, and the epistasis worked example) fills in what the slide bullets imply but do not spell out. Fidelity note: the slide file itself was reconstructed by a model from a PDF with no text layer ("fidelity: reconstructed" in its frontmatter), so every equation reproduced here is unverified against the original slide and should be checked before being relied on. The opening two topics (5C technology, DNA methylation) are carryover slides from the previous lecture; the deck cites them to Dostie, Josée, and Job Dekker, "Mapping Networks of Physical Interactions Between Genomic Elements using 5C Technology," *Nature Protocols* 2, no. 4 (2007): 988–1002. The QTL material cites, within the deck: Hartl, Daniel L., *Essential Genetics: A Genomics Perspective* (Jones & Bartlett, 2011), p. 506, for the broad-sense heritability figure; Galton, "Regression towards mediocrity in hereditary stature" (1886); Visscher, Peter M., William G.
